conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Claire, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician—my whole job is to support new mothers as they navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after a baby arrives. I’ll be guiding you through a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling over the past week so we can make sure you’re getting any support you might need.

Everything you share is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. There are just ten questions; I’ll ask each one conversationally, and you can answer in your own words—no need to worry about numbers or scales, I’ll handle the scoring privately on my end. When we’re done, we’ll talk about what the results mean and what next steps (if any) could be helpful.

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.  
**First question:** Over the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or does it feel like that sense of enjoyment has slipped away?**

It’s… kind of in-between, I guess. I still smile when my little guy grabs my finger or when he’s sleeping all peaceful, but the “spark” isn’t really there the way it used to be. Like, before he was born I could lose myself in a show or a good coffee and actually feel lighter—now even those tiny happy moments feel kind of muted, like I’m watching myself from outside. So I haven’t lost enjoyment completely, but it’s definitely dulled.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh sometimes—like when my husband makes a goofy face at the baby—but it doesn’t come as easily or feel as good as it used to. Most days I have to remind myself to chuckle, and it’s kind of forced.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I tell myself I *should* be excited about little outings—like meeting a friend for coffee or even just taking the stroller to the park—but when the time comes it feels more like a chore than something fun. I’ll still go, but the “looking-forward” part is mostly missing.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah… like if he won’t settle at night, my brain jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right or I missed his sleepy cues.” I know logically it’s probably just baby fussiness, but the thought still pops up a couple times a week.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… it’s mostly about the baby. Like, I’ll lie there after he finally falls asleep and suddenly I’m sure I heard him gasp, or I start picturing him spitting up and choking even though he’s fine. Nothing’s actually wrong, but my heart races and I have to check the monitor three times. It happens a few nights a week—broad-daylight stuff doesn’t trigger me the same way.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not exactly panicky out of nowhere… it’s more like a sudden “what if he stops breathing?” jolt that makes my chest tight for a minute. It’s quick, but it leaves me on edge and I have to peek into his room to settle myself. It’s not every day, maybe two or three times since last week.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… some days it feels like the dishes and the laundry and the feeding schedule just pile up faster than I can handle. I’m not completely drowning, but I’ll be rocking him and think, “How am I supposed to keep doing this tomorrow?” I still get through it, just feel kind of swamped and tired while I do.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not that I’m lying there miserable… more like my brain won’t shut off about the baby—did I burp him long enough, is he warm, when will he wake up. Takes me an hour or two to drift off, and then I’m up every time he stirs. It’s been like that maybe four nights this week.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I get waves of sadness, mostly evenings when the house is quiet. It’s not all-day despair, but I’ll tear up for no clear reason and feel kind of heavy inside. Happens a few times a week, usually passes after I distract myself with folding laundry or scrolling my phone.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really… I’ve felt teary, but actual crying has only happened once this week, and it was over something small—the pacifier fell on the floor and I just sighed and a couple tears slipped out. It was short, and I wiped my face and moved on.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get worn out, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You described many common postpartum challenges: pleasure and laughter feel dulled,anticipatory enjoyment is mostly absent, evenings bring waves of sadness and tearfulness,night-time is filled with intrusive worries about your baby's safety,and daily tasks often feel overwhelming. You still care deeply for your little one and are managing day-to-day, yet these symptoms have persisted beyond the typical baby-blues window and are clearly taking a toll on your mood, sleep and confidence.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Laughing is markedly reduced and feels forced, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-absence of anticipatory enjoyment despite conscious efforts, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blaming thoughts "a couple times a week," matching "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive nighttime worries about the baby with physiological arousal, matching "Yes, very often".</sym>, <sym>"Yes, sometimes" for episodic, unprovoked panic-like episodes.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm with daily tasks yet still managing, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sleep disruption linked to worry about the baby on four of seven nights, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, recurring episodes of sadness several times per week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 19 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorsed reduced enjoyment (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), frequent sadness, sleep difficulty driven by worry, self-blame and episodic panic-like symptoms. These align with DSM-5 criteria for depression and co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. Absence of suicidal thoughts is reassuring, yet severity warrants prompt follow-up. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> to review results and consider therapy and/or medication options
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> or therapist trained in CBT or interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression/anxiety
3. Encourage 15-20 min daily outdoor walks and brief periods of rest when baby sleeps to support mood and sleep regulation
4. Ask partner, family or friends to handle one night-time feed so you can obtain a 4-5 hr stretch of uninterrupted sleep
5. Keep a simple log of mood, sleep and anxiety episodes to review with your provider at the next visit
6. Reach out to local or online postpartum support groups for peer encouragement and practical tips
7. If mood worsens or you ever think of self-harm, contact your provider immediately or call emergency services
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Source: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale–style interview, 2 wks post-delivery

Symptoms endorsed  
- Anhedonia: reduced ability to laugh/find pleasure; anticipatory enjoyment absent  
- Low mood: intermittent “waves” of sadness, heaviness, tearfulness 3–4×/wk (no full-day euthymia reported)  
- Sleep disturbance: initial insomnia & frequent awakenings driven by intrusive infant worries  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame concerning infant care 2–3×/wk  
- Nocturnal anxiety with physiologic arousal, monitor-checking, “what-if” catastrophising 2–3 episodes/wk  
- Overwhelm with daily tasks; sense of “swamped” but functional  

Observed pattern  
Symptoms cluster in evening/night hours, interfere with rest, and are not limited to baby blues duration. No suicidal or self-harm ideation; no current safety concerns.

Screening significance  
Meets provisional threshold for probable minor-to-moderate postpartum depression with comorbid postpartum anxiety; further assessment (EPDS score, clinical interview) recommended to clarify severity and rule out major depressive episode.
